skill.name: ffind
skill.description: Analyze firmware files, identify file types, and optionally extract embedded ext2, ext3, ext4, or F2FS filesystems with the iothackbot ffind tool.
skill.summary: Find file types and extract supported filesystems from firmware images.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: Eighteen external-command alerts are false positives caused by Markdown formatting, not Ruby backtick execution. Four sudo instructions are confirmed because extraction runs firmware tooling with root privileges; two temporary extraction paths add shared-directory risk. No prompt injection, exfiltration, or hidden execution instructions were found.

remediation.suggestion: Run analysis unprivileged by default. Require explicit confirmation before sudo, then isolate extraction in a disposable container or virtual machine.
Create a private temporary directory with restrictive permissions, reject symlinks, and avoid fixed paths under /tmp.

content.value_statement: Firmware images can hide filesystems and security artifacts that are difficult to locate. This skill guides ffind analysis, type detection, and optional filesystem extraction.
actual_capabilities: Analyze one or more file paths with ffind and summarize detected types.
Request artifact-only results or include all file types with the -a option.
Enable verbose diagnostics with the -v option.
Extract ext2, ext3, ext4, and F2FS filesystems with the -e option.
Choose text, JSON, or quiet output formats.
Direct extracted content to a custom output directory with the -d option.
limitations: The iothackbot ffind binary must be installed and selected instead of The Sleuth Kit command with the same name.
Filesystem extraction requires root privileges and external packages such as e2fsprogs, f2fs-tools, and util-linux.
The documented extraction support is limited to ext2, ext3, ext4, and F2FS filesystems.
Processing untrusted firmware as root should occur inside an isolated disposable environment.

use_cases.title: Triage a firmware image
use_cases.description: Identify embedded file types and security artifacts before deciding whether extraction is necessary.

use_cases.title: Extract an IoT root filesystem
use_cases.description: Extract a supported filesystem into a controlled directory for configuration and binary review.

use_cases.title: Compare firmware build contents
use_cases.description: Analyze several images with consistent options and summarize differences in detected file types.

prompt_templates.title: Identify firmware artifacts
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze [firmware path] with ffind. Report detected artifact types, do not extract files, and verify that the iothackbot ffind binary is selected.

prompt_templates.title: Show every detected type
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze [path] with ffind and include all file types. Summarize the main categories and note any filesystem images.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare a controlled extraction
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare to extract supported filesystems from [firmware path] into [output directory]. Verify dependencies, explain sudo use, and request confirmation before execution.

prompt_templates.title: Compare multiple firmware images
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze [image one] and [image two] with verbose output. Compare detected filesystems and security artifacts, then recommend targeted follow-up inspection.

output_examples.output: The analysis identifies the main file categories, highlights embedded filesystem signatures, and recommends whether deeper extraction is warranted.

output_examples.input: Extract supported filesystems from device.img into a controlled workspace.
output_examples.output: The response verifies the correct ffind binary and dependencies, explains privilege requirements, requests confirmation, and summarizes extracted locations after completion.

output_examples.input: Compare two firmware images and show all detected types.
output: A concise inventory for each image.
A comparison of filesystem and artifact differences.
Suggested directories or binaries for further review.

best_practices: Verify the absolute path and help output of the iothackbot ffind binary before analysis.
Start with unprivileged type detection and request explicit confirmation before any sudo extraction.
Use a private output directory inside an isolated environment when processing untrusted firmware.
anti_patterns: Do not run an unverified ffind command because The Sleuth Kit provides a different binary with the same name.
Do not extract untrusted images as root directly on a production workstation.
Do not write privileged extraction output into a fixed shared temporary directory.

faq.question: What does this skill analyze?
faq.answer: It analyzes files and directories, identifies file types, and highlights artifacts relevant to firmware and IoT security review.

faq.question: Which filesystems can it extract?
faq.answer: The documented extraction support covers ext2, ext3, ext4, and F2FS filesystems.

faq.question: Does basic analysis require sudo?
faq.answer: The instructions require sudo for extraction, not for ordinary file-type analysis.

faq.question: Which external tools are required?
faq.answer: Extraction depends on e2fsprogs, f2fs-tools, and util-linux.

faq.question: How do I avoid the ffind name collision?
faq.answer: Check ffind help output and invoke the iothackbot binary by its absolute repository path when another ffind is installed.

faq.question: Can it analyze multiple files?
faq.answer: Yes. The documented command accepts multiple paths and can include all detected types with the -a option.
